variants.title: Run the hybrid training loop
variants.context: Near-term QML is hybrid. Classical code prepares a bounded input, the device executes parameterized circuits, repeated shots estimate loss and gradients with uncertainty, and a classical optimizer proposes parameters and checks stopping criteria.
variants.prompt: A variational classifier trains on encoded feature vectors. Put one iteration of the loop in order.

items.text: Estimate loss and gradients by aggregating repeated shots with their uncertainty.
Update and decide classically: propose new parameters, check stopping criteria, and compare with the baseline.
Prepare a bounded input classically, recording preparation time, fidelity assumptions, and any compression.
Execute the parameterized circuits after compiling to the device topology, retaining calibration and queue metadata.

variants.hint: Which stages does classical infrastructure still own?
variants.explanation: Classical code owns preparation, orchestration, optimization, and evaluation, while the device evaluates only the selected circuits.

variants.title: Run the hybrid training loop
variants.context: Near-term QML is hybrid. Classical code prepares a bounded input, the device executes parameterized circuits, repeated shots estimate loss and gradients with uncertainty, and a classical optimizer proposes parameters and checks stopping criteria.
variants.prompt: Parameter-shift gradients are enabled, so each parameter needs several circuit evaluations. Put the iteration in order.

items.text: Estimate the gradient from the shifted circuit results and report its uncertainty, not just its mean.
Update and decide whether the step is informative enough to continue or the run should stop.
Prepare the same bounded input so every shifted circuit sees identical encoding.
Execute the full set of shifted parameterized circuits on the device, keeping queue and calibration metadata.

variants.hint: The gradient is estimated, so it arrives with an interval attached.
variants.explanation: Parameter-shift methods multiply circuit executions per step, which is why the gradient's uncertainty is part of the stopping decision.

variants.title: Run the hybrid training loop
variants.context: Near-term QML is hybrid. Classical code prepares a bounded input, the device executes parameterized circuits, repeated shots estimate loss and gradients with uncertainty, and a classical optimizer proposes parameters and checks stopping criteria.
variants.prompt: Error mitigation is added, multiplying executions per circuit. Put the iteration in order for that configuration.

items.text: Execute each circuit together with its mitigation variants on the device.
Estimate the mitigated expectation and report the reduced bias alongside the extra executions it cost.
Update and decide whether the quality gain justifies the multiplied execution budget.
Prepare the bounded input and record what the mitigation configuration assumes about it.

variants.hint: Mitigation buys a less biased estimate with something.
variants.explanation: Error mitigation reduces bias by spending more executions, so its cost belongs in the same budget as shots and gradients.

variants.title: Budget the measurements
variants.context: Measurement returns samples, not amplitudes. For an observable with outcomes plus one and minus one the independent-shot variance is 1 minus the expectation squared, and sampling error falls roughly with the square root of the shot count.
variants.prompt: A variational model has 24 trainable parameters. Parameter-shift needs 2 circuit evaluations per parameter, and each evaluation uses 1,000 shots. How many shots does one full gradient estimate consume?
variants.hint: Count circuits first, then shots per circuit.
variants.explanation: Parameter-shift gradients cost two circuit evaluations per trainable parameter, so shot budgets grow with model size before any mitigation is added.

mistakes.feedback: That charges one shifted circuit per parameter instead of the two parameter-shift requires.
That is the number of circuit evaluations, not the shots those evaluations consume.

variants.title: Budget the measurements
variants.context: Measurement returns samples, not amplitudes. For an observable with outcomes plus one and minus one the independent-shot variance is 1 minus the expectation squared, and sampling error falls roughly with the square root of the shot count.
variants.prompt: An observable with outcomes plus one and minus one has an estimated expectation of 0.6. What is the independent-shot variance?
variants.explanation: The independent-shot variance is 1 minus the expectation squared, so a signal near zero is the most expensive one to resolve.

mistakes.feedback: That computes 1 minus the expectation and skips the square.
That is the expectation squared on its own, not the variance.

variants.title: Budget the measurements
variants.context: Measurement returns samples, not amplitudes. For an observable with outcomes plus one and minus one the independent-shot variance is 1 minus the expectation squared, and sampling error falls roughly with the square root of the shot count.
variants.prompt: A run used 2,000 shots per circuit and its confidence interval is three times wider than needed. Under the independent-shot model, how many shots per circuit are required to make the interval one third as wide?
variants.hint: Sampling error falls with the square root of the shot count.
variants.explanation: Shrinking an interval by a factor needs the square of that factor in shots, so a threefold reduction costs nine times the measurements.

mistakes.feedback: That scales shots linearly with the interval, but error falls only with the square root of shots.
That doubles the shots, which narrows the interval by about 1.4 times rather than 3.

variants.title: Locate the bottleneck
variants.context: The bottleneck moves between iterations. A run can be encoding-bound, queue-bound, shot-bound, optimization-bound, or classical-bound, and the fix for one of those does nothing for the others.
variants.prompt: A hybrid run is profiled end to end. Match each bottleneck to what it means.

pairs.label: Encoding-bound
pairs.detail: State preparation costs more than the circuit manages to save.

pairs.label: Queue-bound
pairs.detail: Remote hardware latency dominates an otherwise small computation.

pairs.label: Shot-bound
pairs.detail: Many observables, gradients, or mitigation variants multiply executions.

pairs.label: Optimization-bound
pairs.detail: Noisy gradients or barren plateaus force too many iterations.

pairs.label: Classical-bound
pairs.detail: Preprocessing, decoding, or baseline search dominates total time.

variants.hint: Ask which stage of the loop the wall clock is actually sitting in.
variants.explanation: Naming the bottleneck decides the fix, because more shots cannot repair an encoding cost and a faster queue cannot repair a flat gradient.

variants.title: Locate the bottleneck
variants.context: The bottleneck moves between iterations. A run can be encoding-bound, queue-bound, shot-bound, optimization-bound, or classical-bound, and the fix for one of those does nothing for the others.
variants.prompt: Four teams report the same symptom of slow progress. Match each observation to the bottleneck behind it.

pairs.label: Elapsed time is dominated by waiting for a shared device
pairs.detail: Queue-bound, since remote latency dwarfs the computation.

pairs.label: Loading each classical record into a state costs more than the circuit
pairs.detail: Encoding-bound, since preparation eats the proposed gain.

pairs.label: Gradients hover near zero as the circuit family grows
pairs.detail: Optimization-bound, since barren plateaus stall the search.

pairs.label: Adding mitigation variants tripled executions at unchanged depth
pairs.detail: Shot-bound, since executions multiply per estimate.

variants.hint: Two of these have nothing to do with the circuit itself.
variants.explanation: The bottleneck moves between iterations, so profiling has to attribute elapsed time to preparation, queue, shots, optimization, and classical work.

variants.title: Locate the bottleneck
variants.context: The bottleneck moves between iterations. A run can be encoding-bound, queue-bound, shot-bound, optimization-bound, or classical-bound, and the fix for one of those does nothing for the others.
variants.prompt: Each team proposes a fix. Match the proposed fix to the bottleneck it can actually address.

pairs.label: Compress the features before state preparation
pairs.detail: Encoding-bound, where preparation cost is the binding constraint.

pairs.label: Batch jobs and reserve device time
pairs.detail: Queue-bound, where waiting dominates the elapsed time.

pairs.label: Group commuting observables to share measurements
pairs.detail: Shot-bound, where executions per estimate are the cost.

pairs.label: Switch to an optimizer built for noisy loss estimates
pairs.detail: Optimization-bound, where noisy gradients stall progress.

variants.hint: A fix aimed at the wrong stage leaves the wall clock unchanged.
variants.explanation: Each remedy targets one stage, so the profile has to identify the binding stage before any optimization work is chosen.

variants.title: Design the experiment
variants.context: A responsible study establishes a classical floor, validates the circuit on a simulator, profiles the complete hardware path, and scales only the narrow hypothesis that survived matched quality, repeated trials, and a competitive baseline.
variants.prompt: A team proposes a quantum kernel method for a classification task. Put the study steps in order.

items.text: Scale only the narrow claim that survived matched quality, repeated trials, and the competitive baseline.
Validate the circuit on a simulator, checking encoding, observables, gradients, and small-instance behavior.
Profile the complete hardware path: compilation, queues, shots, mitigation, retries, and output processing.
Establish a classical floor by tuning an appropriate model and recording quality, compute, and search budget.

variants.hint: Which step has to happen before anyone knows what winning would mean?
variants.explanation: The classical floor is set first, because a result with no tuned comparator cannot be interpreted no matter how it was measured.

variants.title: Design the experiment
variants.context: A responsible study establishes a classical floor, validates the circuit on a simulator, profiles the complete hardware path, and scales only the narrow hypothesis that survived matched quality, repeated trials, and a competitive baseline.
variants.prompt: A promising simulator result is being pushed straight to a hardware claim. Put the steps in order for doing it properly.

items.text: Scale only if the same narrow claim survives repeated hardware trials against that baseline.
Keep the simulator run as correctness evidence rather than as a performance result.
Establish the classical floor at the same quality target the claim will use.
Profile the complete hardware path, keeping simulator and hardware evidence separate in the report.

variants.hint: What can a simulator establish, and what can it not?
variants.explanation: Simulator evidence establishes feasibility and correctness, so it is reported separately from hardware evidence rather than merged into one claim.

variants.title: Design the experiment
variants.context: A responsible study establishes a classical floor, validates the circuit on a simulator, profiles the complete hardware path, and scales only the narrow hypothesis that survived matched quality, repeated trials, and a competitive baseline.
variants.prompt: The first hardware profile shows the method losing to the classical floor. Put the steps in order for handling that result.

items.text: Recheck the simulator run to isolate whether the gap is device noise or an encoding assumption.
Decline to scale, and record which assumption failed before designing a larger experiment.
Publish the complete profile including failed runs, seeds, and calibration context.
Confirm the classical floor was tuned fairly and its search budget was recorded.

variants.hint: A negative result with a trustworthy benchmark is still a useful milestone.
variants.explanation: A well-instrumented negative result identifies the assumption that failed and prevents a larger experiment from optimizing the wrong boundary.

variants.title: Keep the claim narrow
variants.context: Different claims must not be collapsed. Hardness of simulation is not a solved task, a tiny-dataset accuracy win is not a computational advantage, an asymptotic speedup may begin beyond useful sizes, and logical operations are not wall-clock time.
variants.prompt: A team shows its circuit family is hard to simulate classically and proposes announcing a machine learning advantage. What is the accurate reading?
options: Simulation hardness is evidence about the circuit, not about any learning task being solved better.
The advantage holds for this dataset size but should be restated once larger data is available.
The result is sound if the classical comparator is a generic state-vector simulator at the same depth.
optionFeedback: Correct: a circuit can be hard to simulate without solving a useful task, so those two claims stay separate.
Restating a claim at a larger size does not rescue evidence that never concerned a learning task.
Choosing a weak simulator as the comparator makes the claim less credible rather than more.
variants.hint: Ask which question the hardness result actually answers.
variants.explanation: Hardness of simulation, tiny-dataset accuracy, asymptotic speedup, and wall-clock time are four different claims that must not be merged.

variants.title: Keep the claim narrow
variants.context: Different claims must not be collapsed. Hardness of simulation is not a solved task, a tiny-dataset accuracy win is not a computational advantage, an asymptotic speedup may begin beyond useful sizes, and logical operations are not wall-clock time.
variants.prompt: A study benchmarks against brute-force state-vector simulation, but a tensor-network method handles this circuit family far more efficiently. What must change?
options: Keep the state-vector comparator and note the tensor-network method as related future work.
Report both comparators and let readers decide which classical method is the relevant one.
Compare against the best applicable classical method, since the classical baseline is a moving target.
optionFeedback: Deferring the stronger method to future work leaves the current claim resting on a comparator that is already beaten.
Presenting a weak comparator alongside a strong one still frames the weak one as a legitimate benchmark.
Correct: tensor-network, stabilizer, and problem-specific simulators are part of the baseline the claim has to beat.
variants.hint: Which classical method would a skeptical reviewer reach for?
variants.explanation: The classical baseline is a moving target, so a claim compares against the best applicable method rather than brute-force simulation.

variants.title: Keep the claim narrow
variants.context: Different claims must not be collapsed. Hardness of simulation is not a solved task, a tiny-dataset accuracy win is not a computational advantage, an asymptotic speedup may begin beyond useful sizes, and logical operations are not wall-clock time.
variants.prompt: A resource estimate counts logical qubits and logical operations for a fault-tolerant algorithm and converts that directly into a runtime figure. What is missing?
options: Shot counts and mitigation variants have not been added to the logical operation total yet.
Queue time and compilation on the target service have not been included in the runtime figure.
Physical-qubit overhead, magic-state production, decoding, and error-correction cycles are unaccounted for.
optionFeedback: Shots and mitigation belong to near-term hybrid budgets, not to a fault-tolerant logical resource estimate.
Queueing matters for near-term device access and is not what makes a logical count differ from a runtime.
Correct: physical overhead, magic states, and decoding can dominate, so logical complexity and hardware estimation stay separate artifacts.
variants.hint: What sits between a logical operation and a physical machine?
variants.explanation: Fault-tolerant reasoning happens in logical qubits, and the physical resource estimate is a separate artifact that can dominate the result.
